passage:
On the edge of Nashik, Jahnavi ran a small tailoring unit from the front room of her house, and her old sewing machine had finally died. Her brother Akash arrived with a pile of brochures: fifteen machines from the dealer in town.
Jahnavi pushed most of them aside. "First, what do I need?" On the back of a bill she wrote: sews thick cloth, can be fixed at the local repair shop, fits the budget.
Only three brochures passed. She rode to the dealer, tried those three, and bought the second one, though Akash pointed at a shinier model.
"It does what I need," she said. By evening she was hemming blouses on it.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi write on the back of the bill?
qa.a: Sews thick cloth, can be fixed at the local repair shop, fits the budget.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi ignore the shinier model?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt confident and satisfied because the second machine met every need on her list, and she did not want extra shine to pull her back into searching.

qa.q: What would you tell a friend who has fifteen options, based on Jahnavi's approach?
qa.a: Write down what you truly need first, keep only the options that pass, try a few, and buy the one that does the job.

qa.q: How might Akash see his sister's quick choice?
qa.a: Akash may be surprised she ignored most of his brochures and the shiny model, but seeing her hemming by evening shows him her way worked.

grounding: Shows a young woman who writes criteria first, narrows to three and picks a good-enough machine.

passage:
In a rented room in Manchester, Jin had forty-one second-hand bikes saved on a listing site. Chidi, a flatmate, looked over and laughed. "You'll still be scrolling at Christmas."
Jin closed the laptop and took a sheet of paper. "Okay. Three things: gears for the hills, a lock included, under a hundred and fifty pounds." Twenty minutes later there were five. Jin kept the three nearest and went to see them on Saturday with Chidi.
The second bike had a scratched frame but ticked every box. "Good enough," Jin said, and paid. Riding home along the canal, Jin didn't open the listings again.

qa.q: How many bikes did Jin have saved at first?
qa.a: Jin had forty-one second-hand bikes saved on a listing site.

qa.q: What does 'Good enough' tell us about how Jin felt?
qa.a: Jin felt satisfied and calm, because a bike that met the three needs was the goal, so the scratched frame didn't matter and there was no urge to keep hunting.

qa.q: Which moment was Jin's turning point, and why?
qa.a: Closing the laptop to write three criteria, because it turned forty-one options into five and then three to visit.

qa.q: How might Chidi view the change on Saturday?
qa.a: Chidi, who joked about scrolling till Christmas, may be impressed to see Jin buy a bike in one morning.

grounding: Shows a young adult who sets three criteria, shortlists three bikes and settles on a good-enough one.

passage: The community centre in Hyderabad's Old City had one week to book a ground for the youth football day. Zainab, the new volunteer, arrived at Rehana's desk with a printout of nineteen grounds. "This one has floodlights, this one's near the bus depot, this one's the cheapest..." Rehana smiled and opened her notebook. "Before we look at any, what must it have?" Together they wrote three things: walking distance for the kids, toilets that work, and within the budget. Fifteen grounds dropped away. Rehana circled three of the four left. "Any of these is good enough. The school ground has shade. Let's call them now." Zainab glanced at the floodlit stadium. "But that one's really nice." "It's also across town. The kids won't get there." By lunch the booking was done.

qa.q: What three things did Rehana and Zainab write down?
qa.a: Walking distance for the kids, toilets that work, and within the budget.

qa.q: Why was Zainab still drawn to the floodlit stadium?
qa.a: It looked like the best option on paper, and Zainab didn't want to give up something so impressive, even though it was across town.

qa.q: Which step made the decision quick, and why did it work?
qa.a: Writing the must-haves before looking at any ground cut nineteen options to four, so they only had to compare a few good-enough ones.

qa.q: How might the kids coming to the football day be affected by the choice of the school ground?
qa.a: They could walk there easily and play in the shade, so more of them would turn up and enjoy the day than at a far-off stadium.

grounding: A young coordinator sets criteria first, keeps a shortlist of three and books a good-enough ground instead of chasing the perfect one.

passage:
Subject: How I finally chose the laptop

Hi Hrithik,
You asked how I picked a laptop without losing my mind, since you've been stuck on yours for a month. Here's what I did.
Before opening a single website, I wrote what I actually need: runs design software smoothly, battery for a full workday, within my budget. That's it. Not the thinnest, not the newest.
Then I let myself look at only three that met all three points. When a colleague sent me a fourth "amazing deal", I didn't open it. I picked the one with the better keyboard, because I type all day. Is it the perfect laptop? Probably not. Is it good enough? Yes, and I've stopped thinking about it.
Try it, little brother. Three needs, three options, one evening.
Tejas Bhaiya

qa.q: What did Tejas write down before opening a single website?
qa.a: Runs design software smoothly, battery for a full workday, and within his budget.

qa.q: Why didn't Tejas open the fourth "amazing deal" his colleague sent?
qa.a: He felt his three good options were enough and expected that adding more would only bring back doubt, just when he had stopped thinking about it.

qa.q: Which part of Tejas's method could help Hrithik most, and why?
qa.a: Writing needs before browsing, because it lets Hrithik drop most laptops at once instead of comparing them for another month.

qa.q: What might Hrithik feel reading this email after a month of being stuck?
qa.a: He might feel relieved and a little embarrassed, and hopeful that a simple plan could end his search in one evening 🙂

grounding: An older brother explains how setting criteria, limiting himself to three options and accepting good enough ended his search.

passage: Yash, you asked how I found a flat in two weekends when you've been looking for two months. Honestly? I stopped looking for the perfect one. I'm Simran, and in the first week I did it your way: fifty listings, twenty visits planned, spreadsheets. By Friday I was dizzy. So I sat down and wrote three rules before opening a single listing: under thirty minutes to the office, morning light in the bedroom, a lane I'd feel safe walking at night. Everything else was a bonus. Then I only visited places that passed all three, and I stopped at three. The second one had a tiny kitchen, but everything else was right. I took it that day. Do I wonder about the others? A little. But I'm happy. Good enough, it turns out, is really good.

qa.q: What were Simran's three rules for a flat?
qa.a: Under thirty minutes to the office, morning light in the bedroom, and a lane safe to walk at night.

qa.q: How did Simran feel by the Friday of the first week, and what changed?
qa.a: Simran felt dizzy and overwhelmed by fifty listings, then calmer after setting three rules and a limit of three visits.

qa.q: Which part of Simran's method could Yash use right away?
qa.a: Writing a few must-haves before looking, visiting only places that pass them, stopping after three, and taking a good-enough one.

qa.q: How might Yash feel hearing Simran's story after two months of searching?
qa.a: Yash might feel a bit frustrated but also relieved to hear a simpler way that could end the search.

grounding: Shows a young professional setting criteria first, limiting the search to three visits, and choosing a good-enough flat.

passage: I'm Sarika, Sudha's younger sister, and I watched her plan her own wedding food in one afternoon after Mummy had been stuck for a month. Mummy had a folder of twenty-two caterers. Sudha took the folder, sat at the dining table and wrote on the first page: 'Veg. Good dal. Fits our budget. Nobody we've quarrelled with before.' Then she went through the folder and crossed out anything that failed even one line. Seven survived. She rang the first three and booked tastings for Saturday. At the tasting she picked the second one, a small family business with the best dal. Mummy asked, "But what about the others?" Sudha shrugged. "This one's good." I couldn't tell if she was calm inside, but she slept well that night, which is more than Mummy had done in weeks.

qa.q: How many caterers were in Mummy's folder?
qa.a: There were twenty-two caterers in the folder.

qa.q: What do Sudha's shrug and good sleep suggest about how Sudha felt after choosing?
qa.a: They suggest Sudha felt settled and content with a good-enough choice, though Sarika couldn't be sure what was going on inside.

qa.q: Which step in Sudha's approach cut the folder down most, and why does it work?
qa.a: Writing four must-haves first and crossing out any caterer that failed one, because clear criteria shrink a huge list before any comparing begins.

qa.q: How had the month of searching been for Mummy?
qa.a: Mummy had been stuck and sleeping badly, weighed down by twenty-two options with no way to narrow them.

grounding: Shows, through a sister's eyes, a young woman setting criteria first, testing a shortlist of three, and choosing a good-enough caterer.

passage:
Monday. Chetan had forty laptop models open and a headache. His old one had died, and his freelance design work couldn't wait long. He closed the laptop lid with nothing chosen.
Wednesday. Over chai, his friend Kamal made him write three things on a napkin: a good screen for colour work, light enough to carry to clients, within his budget. "Now only three models. No more tabs." Chetan found three that fit and planned a shop visit for the weekend.
The next Saturday. At the store he tried all three, liked the second one's screen best, and bought it in twenty minutes. That night he sent Kamal a photo of his first finished design on it. "Good enough," he wrote, "is actually great."

qa.q: What three things did Chetan write on the napkin?
qa.a: A good screen for colour work, light enough to carry to clients, and within his budget.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel on Monday, and how had that changed by Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday Chetan felt overwhelmed, with a headache from forty models; by Saturday he felt satisfied with a quick, good-enough choice.

qa.q: Why did the napkin list make the decision easier?
qa.a: Setting criteria first cut forty models to three, so comparing became quick and there was little to regret.

qa.q: What might Kamal have felt getting the photo that night?
qa.a: Kamal probably felt pleased and a little proud that the napkin idea worked.

grounding: Shows a young freelancer setting criteria, limiting the choice to three laptops, and picking a good-enough one.

passage:
Nirmala, you asked how I chose this flat. Let your Anirban mama tell you. When I was about twenty-five, I spent six months looking at houses in Kolkata. Every Sunday I saw five, six places. Each one had something wrong, a small kitchen or a far bus stop. I lost two good flats because I wanted to see just one more.

Then my old boss said, "Write three things you can't live without. Look at only the flats with those, and pick the first good one." I wrote: near the tram, two windows, under my budget. In two weeks I had three flats on my list. I took the second. It wasn't perfect; the stairs are steep even now. But I lived there happily for twelve years.

qa.q: What three things did Anirban write down?
qa.a: Anirban wrote near the tram, two windows, under my budget.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel during the six months of searching, and why?
qa.a: Anirban likely felt frustrated and stuck, since every flat had something wrong and two good ones slipped away while Anirban wanted to see one more.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Anirban's search?
qa.a: The turning point was Anirban writing three must-haves, as the old boss suggested, and choosing a good flat from a shortlist of three.

qa.q: How might Anirban's old boss have seen his months of searching?
qa.a: The boss probably saw Anirban wearing out chasing a perfect flat and wanted to offer a simpler way to decide.

grounding: An elder recalls how setting criteria, keeping a shortlist of three and picking a good-enough option ended months of searching.

Nikita had until 5 p.m. to book a venue for her team's offsite, and the office Wi-Fi kept dropping. Her colleague Mahima had forwarded nineteen options.

Nikita closed the long thread and opened a blank note. First: under forty minutes from the office, a room for twenty-five, lunch included. Only then did she scroll again. Nine venues failed at once. She rang the remaining ones between Wi-Fi cuts and kept three that could confirm today.

At 4:20 Mahima asked, "What about the lake resort? Photos look amazing."

"It's ninety minutes away," Nikita said. "The second one on my list meets everything. Good enough is good today."

She booked it at 4:35. At the offsite, nobody mentioned the lake.

qa.q: By what time did Nikita have to book the venue?
qa.a: She had until 5 p.m. to book the venue.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel calm turning down the lake resort?
qa.a: She felt confident because her criteria were already set, and the resort failed the distance rule, so she didn't have to agonise.

qa.q: What worked in Nikita's approach, and why?
qa.a: Writing criteria before looking cut nineteen venues to three, which let her decide quickly even with patchy Wi-Fi.

qa.q: How might Mahima see Nikita's choice at first, and later?
qa.a: Mahima may have felt a bit disappointed about the lake at first, then relieved when the offsite went well without it.

grounding: Under time pressure, a young professional sets criteria first, shortlists three and chooses a good-enough venue.

Amandeep had been looking for a used scooter for her commute across Chandigarh. Her brother Chinmay kept sending her listings on a buy-and-sell site: thirty, forty, fifty a week.

On Sunday she sat in the colony park with a notebook. "Chinmay, stop sending. Here's the rule: less than five years old, one owner, a mechanic can check it this week."

He frowned. "But you might miss a better deal."

"I might. I'll also miss another month of autos."

She picked three from the pile that fit. The first had a cracked mirror, the second was smooth and fairly priced. She stopped there and bought it on Tuesday.

A week later Chinmay forwarded a cheaper one. Amandeep glanced at it, smiled and put her phone away.

qa.q: What rules did Amandeep write in her notebook?
qa.a: Less than five years old, one owner, and a mechanic can check it this week.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep smile and put her phone away when Chinmay sent a cheaper scooter?
qa.a: She felt settled and content with her choice, so a new listing didn't pull her back into doubt.

qa.q: What could someone copy from Amandeep's way of buying?
qa.a: Set a few firm criteria first, pick a small shortlist and stop at the first option that fits instead of searching for the perfect one.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay react differently to buying than Amandeep does?
qa.a: Chinmay worries about missing a better deal, while Amandeep cares more about ending the search and getting to work.

grounding: A young adult sets criteria, keeps a shortlist of three and picks a good-enough scooter rather than hunting for the perfect one.

"I've looked at forty flats online," Hemant groaned, scrolling. "Every one has something wrong."
"Stop scrolling," Parul said, picking up a notebook. "What are the three things that actually matter?"
"Near the metro. Under our budget. Some sunlight."
"Good. Everything else is a bonus." She wrote them down. "Now, of the forty, which pass all three?"
Hemant checked. "Seven."
"Pick your top three from those seven. We see all three on Saturday."
"What if the perfect one comes up on Sunday?"
"Then we'll never live anywhere," Parul said. "We're not looking for perfect. We're looking for good enough, and then we're done."
Hemant laughed. "Good enough sounds so sad."
"Good enough with sunlight sounds lovely."

qa.q: How many flats passed all three criteria?
qa.a: Seven flats passed all three.

qa.q: Why does Parul want to stop at 'good enough'?
qa.a: Parul feels calm and practical, knowing the hunt for perfect could go on forever and wear them both out.

qa.q: What are the steps in Parul's method?
qa.a: Set three criteria, keep only flats that pass, shortlist three and visit them on Saturday, then choose a good-enough one.

qa.q: How does Hemant feel about 'good enough'?
qa.a: Hemant is doubtful at first and jokes that it sounds sad, but seems relieved by the plan.

grounding: Shows a wise young adult who sets criteria first, keeps a shortlist of three and aims for good enough rather than perfect.

passage:
When Madhav and I started looking for a wedding venue last year, I did what I always do: I looked at everything. Thirty-one halls in three weeks. I'm Rashmi, and I once spent a whole weekend choosing a kettle, so this was dangerous.
By the third week I was exhausted and angry at every hall for not being perfect.
So I stopped and made rules. First, three criteria: room for two hundred guests, near the station for Madhav's grandparents, free in February. Second, a shortlist of three, no more. Third, the first hall that met all three and felt warm would be the one. No "but maybe there's something better".
The second hall on the shortlist had a mango tree in the courtyard. We booked it that afternoon.
It wasn't perfect. The parking was awful. But I loved it, and I never went back to the list.

qa.q: How many halls did Rashmi look at in three weeks?
qa.a: Rashmi looked at thirty-one halls in three weeks.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel by the third week?
qa.a: Rashmi felt exhausted and angry at every hall for not being perfect.

qa.q: What rules did Rashmi set, and why did they work?
qa.a: Three criteria, a shortlist of three and choosing the first warm hall that met them, which ended the search for perfect.

qa.q: How might Madhav's grandparents experience the chosen hall?
qa.a: They would likely find it easy and comfortable, since being near the station was one of the three criteria.

grounding: Shows a young adult who sets criteria, keeps a shortlist of three and picks a good-enough venue instead of searching for perfect.

passage:
Supervisor's note, research lab, week 6. Written by Sachin, lab supervisor.
Rehana has been choosing a thesis topic for three weeks. On Monday she brought me a list of nineteen possible topics, each with pros and cons, and said she was "nowhere".
I didn't give her a topic. I asked her to set three criteria first. She chose: data she can access this year, a question she genuinely cares about, and something I can supervise.
By Wednesday she had cut the nineteen to four, and then, on her own, to three. She said, "I'll pick the one that's good enough, not the one that might be perfect."
She chose the water-quality study on Friday and has already started collecting samples. She seemed lighter.
Next step: I've asked her to write down the other two and put them away for later, so they stop calling to her.

qa.q: How many possible topics were on Rehana's first list?
qa.a: Rehana's first list had nineteen possible topics.

qa.q: How did Rehana seem after choosing?
qa.a: Rehana seemed lighter and relieved, having picked a good-enough topic instead of chasing a perfect one.

qa.q: Why was setting criteria first a good approach?
qa.a: The three criteria quickly cut nineteen topics to four and then three, making a good-enough choice possible.

qa.q: How did the three weeks look to Sachin?
qa.a: Sachin saw a capable student stuck among too many options, and chose to guide with a question rather than hand over a topic.

grounding: Shows, in a supervisor's note, a young researcher who sets criteria first, shortlists three and picks a good-enough topic.

passage:
Sunday, 14 July
Flat hunting, day three. The old me would have spent six weeks on this and still cried at the end. Today I tried the method properly.
Before opening a single listing, I wrote three must-haves on a sticky note: under forty minutes to the office, a window that opens onto something green, a landlord who replies within a day. Everything else is a nice-to-have.
Jatin kept sending links. "Jahnavi, this one has a rooftop pool!" Not on the sticky note. Deleted.
By noon I had a shortlist of three. Saw all of them by five. The Indiranagar one isn't perfect: small kitchen, noisy road. But it ticks all three.
I paid the token and felt calm. Jatin thinks I rushed. Maybe. But tonight I'm sleeping, not scrolling.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Three must-haves: under forty minutes to the office, a window that opens onto something green, and a landlord who replies within a day.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel after paying the token, and why?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt calm, because the flat ticked all three must-haves, so the small kitchen and noisy road did not reopen the search.

qa.q: What small step made the search manageable?
qa.a: Writing the must-haves before opening any listing, which let Jahnavi delete links like the rooftop pool and reach a shortlist of three by noon.

qa.q: Why might Jatin react differently to the choice?
qa.a: Jatin thinks it was rushed, perhaps because extras like a rooftop pool seemed worth more searching.

grounding: Shows a person setting criteria first, keeping a shortlist of three and choosing a good-enough flat rather than a perfect one.
